plants.name: Colchicum autumnale
plants.description: Just as the leaves of other plants turn, this bulb sends up goblet-shaped lilac-pink flowers straight from bare ground. Its strappy leaves appeared months earlier and have long since died back, so the blooms stand alone like delicate chalices in damp meadows and garden borders.
plants.location: Meadows and gardens across temperate Europe
plants.funFact: Despite its name, it is not a true crocus. It belongs to the lily relatives, and every part of it is highly toxic, containing colchicine, a compound still used in medicine and in plant breeding.

plants.name: Solidago canadensis
plants.description: Tall, arching plumes of tiny golden flowers light up roadsides, old fields and prairie edges at summer's end. The blooms hum with bees, butterflies and hoverflies stocking up before winter.
plants.bloomingSeason: July to September, peaking in late summer and early autumn
plants.location: Eastern and central North America, including the northeastern United States
plants.funFact: Goldenrod is often blamed for hay fever, but its pollen is heavy and sticky and carried by insects. The real culprit is usually ragweed, which blooms at the same time.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: The largest of all proteas, this South African shrub bears dinner-plate-sized flower heads. Rows of silky, pink-tipped bracts surround a crown of fuzzy centre florets, and the whole bloom looks like an artichoke wearing a royal crown.
plants.location: Fynbos of the Western Cape, South Africa, including Kirstenbosch gardens
plants.funFact: The king protea is South Africa's national flower. It belongs to a plant family so ancient that it dates back to when the southern continents were joined in Gondwana.
